summary: Describes the existing, widely used print server protocol used between line printer daemons, both clients and servers. It is informational and not an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for your computer to send a document to a printer on another computer, and to see the print line.

subtitle: How Berkeley Unix print clients talk to a line printer daemon over TCP port 515.

tldr.problem: Berkeley Unix printing used a set of programs (lpr, lpq, lprm, lpc) that talk to a line printer daemon, but the protocol they used was not written down anywhere.
tldr.mechanism: A client opens a TCP connection to port 515 and sends one command: a single-octet code, a queue name and a line feed. To print, it sends a control file that describes the job and a data file that holds the content.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1179 documents this existing, widely used protocol for the record. It is informational only and does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1179 is an Informational memo. It is not an Internet standard, and it has not been obsoleted or updated according to the RFC index data.

sections.title: What the Protocol Describes
sections.content:
Berkeley versions of Unix provide line printer spooling with four programs: lpr (assign to queue), lpq (display the queue), lprm (remove from queue) and lpc (control the queue). They work with an autonomous process called the line printer daemon.

RFC 1179 describes the protocol a client uses to control printing through that daemon. The memo says it is based almost entirely on the work of Robert Knight at Princeton University, who deciphered the Unix lpr protocol. It is for information only and does not specify an Internet standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer has a helper program that looks after the printer. This document writes down the language that other programs use to ask that helper for things.

sections.title: Model and Command Format
sections.content:
A group of hosts request services from a daemon running on one host. Each printing job produces output from one file and has a unique job number between 0 and 999, inclusive. Jobs are requested by users, and user names may not start with a digit.

LPR is a TCP-based protocol. The daemon listens on port 515, and the client's source port must be in the range 721 to 731, inclusive. Every command begins with a single octet code, followed immediately by the ASCII queue name. Any other operands are separated from the queue name by white space, and a line feed ends the command. A new connection must be made for each command given to the daemon.
sections.plainLanguage: Every request is one short line: a number saying what you want, the name of the printer line, and an end mark. You make a fresh phone call for each request.

sections.title: Daemon Commands
sections.content:
There are five top-level commands. Code 01 prints any waiting jobs, and starts the printing process if it is not already running. Codes 03 and 04 ask for the queue state in short or long form. The reply is an ASCII stream that continues until the connection closes, and the request can be limited to given user names or job numbers.

Code 05 removes jobs. It carries the queue, the agent (the user making the request) and an optional list of users or job numbers. If only the agent is given, the currently active job is deleted. Unless the agent is root, a job not owned by the user cannot be deleted, and only root can delete by user name.

Code 02 receives a printer job and is covered in the next section. After it is sent, the client must read an acknowledgement octet: a positive acknowledgement is an octet of zero bits, and any other pattern is a negative one.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask the helper to start printing, show the waiting list, or cancel a job. Only the boss account may cancel other people's jobs.

sections.title: Sending a Job
sections.content:
After the receive-job command, the same connection carries a second level of subcommands until it closes. The client must wait for an acknowledgement after each subcommand. Subcommand 01 aborts the job and removes any files created so far. Subcommand 02 receives a control file and 03 receives a data file. Each gives a byte count and a file name, then the file bytes follow, then an octet of zero bits marks the end, and a second acknowledgement is required.

The control file name should start with cfA and the data file name with dfA, each followed by a three digit job number and the name of the host that built the file. The data file may hold any 8-bit values, and its meaning is decided by the control file. LPR clients SHOULD be able to send the two files in either order. Servers MUST accept the control file first and SHOULD accept the data file first.
sections.plainLanguage: To print, you hand over two things: a note saying how to print, and the pages themselves. After each handover the helper says okay before you go on.

sections.title: Control File Lines
sections.content:
Each control file line starts with one printable, case-sensitive ASCII character that names a function, and the rest of the line is its operand. Lower case commands request actual printing. Upper case commands give parameters or background conditions. Every control file must include H (responsible host) and P (responsible user), plus at least one lower case command to produce any output.

Examples of parameters are C (banner class), J (job name), L (print banner page), M (mail when printed), N (source file name), T (title) and W (output width, default 132). Printing commands select how the data file is treated: f plain text, l text without filtering control characters, o Postscript, d DVI, t troff, n ditroff, p pr format, r FORTRAN carriage control, v Sun raster, g Berkeley plot and c CIF. Code k is reserved for Kerberized clients and servers and z for the Palladium print system.
sections.plainLanguage: The note is a list of short lines. Each line starts with a letter that says what it means, like who sent the job or whether to add a cover page.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that security issues are not discussed in the memo. It does describe one access rule, that only the agent root may delete jobs the user does not own, but it defines no authentication for the user names that clients send.
sections.plainLanguage: The document does not talk about keeping bad guys out. It only says who is allowed to cancel whose jobs.
